tests.name: Quick Check
tests.description: Timed check on Thermopylae & Salamis (480 BC)

questions.question: Q: Why did the Greeks choose to fight at Thermopylae?
questions.correctAnswer: Thermopylae (the Hot Gates) was a narrow coastal pass where the massive Persian army's numbers were less important. A small force could block the pass, preventing the Persians from advancing into central Greece. The Greeks simultaneously defended the strait of Artemisium with their fleet.

questions.question: Q: How were the Greeks defeated at Thermopylae?
questions.correctAnswer: A local Greek named Ephialtes betrayed the Greeks by showing the Persians a mountain path (the Anopaea path) that outflanked the pass. When Leonidas learned the Persians were approaching from behind, he dismissed most of the allied troops but the 300 Spartans and 700 Thespians remained to fight to the death, covering the retreat.

questions.question: Q: How did Themistocles win the Battle of Salamis?
questions.correctAnswer: Themistocles sent a secret message to Xerxes claiming the Greeks were planning to flee. Xerxes sent his fleet into the narrow strait of Salamis to block their escape. In the confined waters, the Persians' numerical advantage was negated and the more manoeuvrable Greek triremes rammed and destroyed much of the Persian fleet.

tests.name: Exam-Style Practice
tests.description: Short-answer practice on Thermopylae & Salamis (480 BC)

questions.question: Q: What was the significance of the 'wooden walls' oracle?
questions.correctAnswer: Before the invasion, Athens consulted the Delphic oracle which gave a terrifying prophecy about Persian destruction, but mentioned 'a wooden wall' would save Athens. Themistocles interpreted this as the Athenian navy (wooden ships), not the Acropolis walls, and persuaded Athens to evacuate the city and rely on the fleet.

questions.question: Q: Why was Salamis more important than Thermopylae?
questions.correctAnswer: Thermopylae was a heroic but costly Greek defeat. Salamis was a decisive Greek victory that destroyed much of the Persian fleet, prevented Xerxes from supplying his army by sea, and forced him to retreat to Asia with most of his forces. It was the turning point of the war.
